items.stem: Section 1 of the (fictional) Public Parks (Safety) Act 2017 provides that "it is an offence to bring a vehicle into a public park". Lucas used an electric wheelchair on the park paths. Apply the literal rule, the golden rule and the mischief rule to advise whether Lucas has committed the offence. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: literal rule: words are given their plain, ordinary meaning even if the result is absurd (Whiteley v Chappell, LNER v Berriman); golden rule: the literal meaning may be modified to avoid an absurd result (R v Allen, narrow approach) or a repugnant one (Re Sigsworth, wide approach); mischief rule: the court asks what problem the Act was passed to remedy (Heydon's Case; Smith v Hughes). Application: literal rule: Lucas would be guilty, since an electric wheelchair may literally be a vehicle; golden rule: Lucas would be not guilty, since excluding disabled people from parks would be an absurd result; mischief rule: the mischief was the danger and disturbance caused to park users by motor traffic; Lucas would be not guilty because a wheelchair user is a park user whom the Act was meant to protect. Conclusion: The outcome depends on the approach taken; a modern court looking at the purpose of the Act would probably find Lucas not guilty.

items.answer: Law: literal rule: words are given their plain, ordinary meaning even if the result is absurd (Whiteley v Chappell, LNER v Berriman); purposive approach: the court looks for the purpose of Parliament and interprets the words to achieve it (Jones v Tower Boot; R (Quintavalle) v Secretary of State for Health); the court may use extrinsic aids such as Hansard (Pepper v Hart) and explanatory notes to identify the purpose. items.stem: The (fictional) Animal Welfare Act 2016 makes it an offence to keep "dogs, cats, rabbits or other animals" in a flat without a licence. Lina keeps a pet ferret in a flat in Dubai without a licence. Explain how the court is likely to interpret "other animals" and whether Lina commits the offence.
items.answer: Law: ejusdem generis: general words after a list of specific words are limited to things of the same kind; Powell v Kempton Park Racecourse (1899): "house, office, room or other place" limited to indoor places; at least two specific words are needed to form a class (Allen v Emmerson 1944). Application: the listed words create a class, so "other animals" is likely to mean other domestic pets of the same kind; a ferret is a small domestic pet like those listed; so a pet ferret is probably covered by the Act. Conclusion: Applying ejusdem generis, Lina probably commits the offence.

items.stem: Section 1 of the (fictional) School Safety Act 2023 provides that "it is an offence for any person to have a knife in a school building". Priya used a kitchen knife to prepare lunches in the school kitchen as a school cook. Advise Priya, explaining how different approaches to interpretation could lead to different outcomes. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: literal rule: words are given their plain, ordinary meaning even if the result is absurd (Whiteley v Chappell, LNER v Berriman); golden rule: the literal meaning may be modified to avoid an absurd result (R v Allen, narrow approach) or a repugnant one (Re Sigsworth, wide approach); mischief rule: the court asks what problem the Act was passed to remedy (Heydon's Case; Smith v Hughes). items.stem: The (fictional) Animal Welfare Act 2019 makes it an offence to keep "lions, tigers, leopards or other animals" in a flat without a licence. Ana keeps a pet hamster in a flat in Accra without a licence. Explain how the court is likely to interpret "other animals" and whether Ana commits the offence. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: ejusdem generis: general words after a list of specific words are limited to things of the same kind; Powell v Kempton Park Racecourse (1899): "house, office, room or other place" limited to indoor places; at least two specific words are needed to form a class (Allen v Emmerson 1944). Application: the listed words create a class, so "other animals" is likely to mean other big cats or similar dangerous wild animals; a hamster is not a dangerous wild animal like those listed; so a pet hamster is probably not covered by the Act. Conclusion: Applying ejusdem generis, Ana probably does not commit the offence.

items.stem: Evaluate the extent to which the literal, golden and mischief rules allow judges to achieve justice.
items.answer: For: the golden rule avoids absurd results (Re Sigsworth); the mischief rule closes loopholes and promotes Parliament's intention (Smith v Hughes, Royal College of Nursing v DHSS); the literal rule respects democracy and gives certainty. Against: the literal rule can cause injustice (LNER v Berriman, Whiteley v Chappell); the golden rule is limited and there is no clear test of absurdity; the mischief rule gives judges wide discretion and may allow them to make law; there is no hierarchy, so judges can choose the rule that gives the result they prefer. Conclusion: The golden and mischief rules allow more just outcomes but at the cost of certainty and democratic legitimacy.

items.answer: Facts: the Statute of Frauds 1677 required contracts for "goods, wares and merchandise" over a value to be in writing, and the contract was for stocks and shares. items.stem: Ines is charged under a section of the (fictional) Public Safety Act 2018, which makes it an offence to "use a vehicle on a footpath". The meaning of the section is unclear, and during the debate on the Bill the minister made a clear statement about its intended meaning. Explain whether the court may look at what the minister said and what other aids it may use. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: Pepper v Hart (1993): Hansard may be used if the Act is ambiguous, the statement was by a minister or promoter and it is clear; other extrinsic aids include explanatory notes, dictionaries and Law Commission reports; intrinsic aids include the long title, preamble, headings and interpretation section. Application: the section is unclear, so the first condition is met; the statement was made by the minister and is clear; the court may therefore consult Hansard, together with the explanatory notes. Conclusion: All three Pepper v Hart conditions appear to be met, so the court may use Hansard to interpret the section.

items.stem: State the facts and the decision in R v Registrar General, ex p Smith (1991).
items.answer: Facts: a man detained in a secure hospital after killing a cell-mate applied for his birth certificate, which the Adoption Act 1976 gave him an absolute right to obtain. items.stem: With reference to decided cases and statutory provisions where relevant, "The rules of statutory interpretation are unpredictable because judges are free to choose which one to apply." Discuss.
items.answer: For: no hierarchy of rules, so outcomes depend on the judge; cases such as LNER v Berriman and Smith v Hughes produce opposite approaches; makes legal advice difficult. Against: the modern purposive approach is now dominant, giving more consistency; aids such as Hansard and explanatory notes help; the literal rule remains the starting point, giving some predictability. Conclusion: There is some unpredictability, but the modern purposive approach and aids reduce it.
